screens.title: Write the engine
screens.prose: Keep one dictionary per side from price to a `deque` of `[id, qty]`, and a dictionary from id to `(side, price)`. A limit order trades against the best opposite levels it crosses, then rests what is left. A market order never rests.

params.title: Event format (prices in whole pence)
lines: [0, id, side, price, qty]   limit order (side 0 buy, 1 sell)
[1, id, side, qty]          market order
[2, id]                     cancel (ignored if id does not rest)
[3, id, new_qty]            amend (ignored if id does not rest)
smaller keeps its place; equal changes nothing;
larger goes to the back of the same level
Every new_qty is at least 1. Ids are unique.
trade = [taker_id, maker_id, price, qty]

screens.question: Write `run_book(events)`, the trades in order, and `levels(events, side)`, the resting levels of one side as `[price, total_qty]`, best first.

widget.solution:
from collections import deque


def _simulate(events):
    books = {0: {}, 1: {}}   # side -> price -> deque of [id, qty]
    where = {}               # id -> (side, price)
    trades = []

    def match(taker, side, qty, limit):
        opp = books[1 - side]
        while qty > 0 and opp:
            best = min(opp) if side == 0 else max(opp)
            if limit is not None and (
                    (side == 0 and best > limit) or (side == 1 and best < limit)):
                break
            queue = opp[best]
            while qty > 0 and queue:
                maker = queue[0]
                fill = min(qty, maker[1])
                trades.append([taker, maker[0], best, fill])
                qty -= fill
                maker[1] -= fill
                if maker[1] == 0:
                    queue.popleft()
                    del where[maker[0]]
            if not queue:
                del opp[best]
        return qty

    for ev in events:
        kind = ev[0]
        if kind == 0:                       # limit order
            _, oid, side, price, qty = ev
            rest = match(oid, side, qty, price)
            if rest > 0:
                books[side].setdefault(price, deque()).append([oid, rest])
                where[oid] = (side, price)
        elif kind == 1:                     # market order
            _, oid, side, qty = ev
            match(oid, side, qty, None)
        elif kind == 2:                     # cancel
            oid = ev[1]
            if oid in where:
                side, price = where.pop(oid)
                queue = books[side][price]
                for k, o in enumerate(queue):
                    if o[0] == oid:
                        del queue[k]
                        break
                if not queue:
                    del books[side][price]
        else:                               # amend
            _, oid, new_qty = ev
            if oid in where:
                side, price = where[oid]
                queue = books[side][price]
                for k, o in enumerate(queue):
                    if o[0] == oid:
                        if new_qty < o[1]:
                            o[1] = new_qty
                        elif new_qty > o[1]:
                            del queue[k]
                            queue.append([oid, new_qty])
                        break
    return trades, books


def run_book(events):
    return _simulate(events)[0]


def levels(events, side):
    book = _simulate(events)[1][side]
    prices = sorted(book, reverse=(side == 0))
    return [[p, sum(o[1] for o in book[p])] for p in prices]

byKey.test-2: Test 2 walks two ask levels, 101 then 102, each at the maker's price.

hints.text: Put the state in one `struct Engine` with an `apply(event)` method.
A `Resting& m = queue.front()` lets you change the front order's quantity in place.
Mirror the Python. `match` loops over the best opposite level, fills from the front and erases filled makers and empty levels. Cancel and amend use `where` and `std::find_if` on the queue.

feedback.correct: The same engine, with sorted maps doing the best-price search.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test, or the compiler's message.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: order 3 sells 3 at 100 against the bid of 5 at 100. The trade is `{3, 1, 100, 3}`.

explain.text: `std::map` keeps prices sorted, so the best level is at one end in $O(\log n)$ per insert. `std::deque` gives cheap pops at the front and pushes at the back. Erasing a whole level when its queue empties keeps `begin()` honest.

screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: Queues make cancel and amend simple; a sorted map finds the best price
Heaps make amend simpler, because a heap reorders itself after each change
options.why: A heap cannot move one order to the back of its price. An amend up needs a real queue per level.

options.text: A plain dict of price to queue finds the best price in $O(1)$
options.why: A plain dict is unordered, so `min(asks)` scans every level. A sorted map keeps it $O(\log n)$.

options.text: Both need a full scan of the book to cancel an order by its id
options.why: The id map gives the order's side and price at once. Only one level's queue is searched.

hints.text: What does an amend up need that a heap cannot give?
It needs the order moved to the back of its own price, behind others at that price.
Queues per level make cancel and amend local. Best price needs a sorted structure; a plain dict scans.

feedback.correct: Queues make the edits local; a sorted map finds the best price fast.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about an amend up and about finding the best price.

byKey.b: You trusted the heap to reorder. It orders by price and time, but cannot move one order behind its equals on request.
byKey.c: You assumed a dict is sorted. `min` over its keys scans every level.
byKey.d: You forgot the id map. It points straight at the level.

explain.text: The Python reference used `min(opp)`, a scan over the levels, which is fine for a test. The C++ `std::map` finds the best level at one end, in $O(\log n)$ per change. Lazy deletion trades a simple cancel for dead entries left in the heap.

screens.question: Which change needs no new field on a resting order?

options.text: Immediate-or-cancel: drop the remainder instead of resting it
Self-trade prevention: stop a trader trading with itself
options.why: To skip a maker with the taker's owner, each resting order must store its owner. That is a new field.

options.text: A time stamp on every amend, for the audit log
options.why: Each resting order must store its time. That changes the data structure.

options.text: None: every one of these changes needs a new field
options.why: Immediate-or-cancel changes only what happens to the remainder, one line after `match`.

hints.text: What does each change need to know about a resting order?
Immediate-or-cancel is about the incoming order only.
IOC replaces "rest what is left" with "drop what is left". The other two need an owner or a time on each resting order.

feedback.correct: IOC changes one line after `match`; the others add a field.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which change needs stored facts about the makers.

byKey.b: You missed the owner. The loop must compare taker and maker owners, so each maker stores one.
byKey.c: You missed the stored time. Each resting order must carry it.
byKey.d: You missed IOC. It is a market order's rule applied to a limit order.

explain.text: IOC is a limit order that never rests, so only the line after `match` changes. Self-trade prevention compares owners inside the loop, and needs the owner stored. Time stamps need a time stored on each resting order.

ideas: Keep a FIFO queue per price level and a sorted map from price to queue per side. A map from id finds where an order rests.
A limit order trades with each level it crosses, oldest first, at the resting price. A limit rests its remainder; a market order drops it.
An amend down keeps its place, and an amend up joins the back of its level. A cancel of an id that does not rest is ignored.
